newsitem.title: ALBANIA: Albania calls for military aid from Europe.
newsitem.headline: Albania calls for military aid from Europe.

text.p: Albania appealed for military help from Europe on Thursday with the country sliding towards anarchy as arms depots across the country were looted and people used the weapons to raid food warehouses.

Gunfire crackled around the capital in an orgy of celebration. Tirana airport was closed after a nearby military base was looted, preventing the evacuation of some foreign embassy staff ordered out by their governments.
As night fell, repeated bursts of shooting could be heard and tracer fire streaked over the city centre.

Three Albanian navy patrol boats put themselves under control of the Italian navy in international waters in the Adriatic, while three Albanian air force helicopters flew to Italy and surrendered. Italian military sources said as many as four more were on their way across the Adriatic.

Albanian opposition leader Fatos Nano, seen as a possible leader to replace President Salih Berisha, was freed from jail along with other prisoners because their safety could no longer be guaranteed, a government minister said.
Nano has been in jail for nearly four years after being convicted on corruption charges that the opposition said were politically motivated.
Berisha and all Albanian political parties called for NATO's European members to provide military assistance to Tirana to restore order in the Balkan country.

The appeal to the Western European Union said all political forces in Albania agreed outside military assistance was needed "to restore the constitutional order and to preserve the country's integrity".
Dutch Foreign Minister Hans van Mierlo said the request being seriously considered but the WEU said it had received no formal request for help from Albania.
A European mediation mission headed by former Austrian leader Franz Vranitzky was due to fly to Tirana to resume efforts to end the chaos, but was postponed until Friday.
Prime Minister Bashkim Fino said he spoke to Vranitzky by telephone and welcomed the envoy's suggestion that he should meet rebel leaders from the south.
In the northern city of Shkoder, until now untouched by the armed rebellion sweeping the country, doctors said five people had died and 50 were wounded as two arms depots were looted.
The industrial city of Elbasan, 55 km (35 miles) south of Tirana, came under rebel control and eyewitnesses reported three people were killed on Thursday by celebratory fire.
Albanian state television listed another four towns in the north and the Southeast where rebels had looted arms.
In Tirana, many shops and businesses closed and women queued for bread at bakeries.
Italy was evacuating some 400 foreign nationals, 330 of them Italians. The evacuees were being ferried to Italian navy ships in the Adriatic by helicopters from two air fields near Durres.
The United States said it had put a naval battle group on standby in the Adriatic Sea and was considering using military forces to evacuate more than 2,000 Americans living in Albania.
Britain said it was planning to evacuate more than 120 British, Irish and Canadian citizens.

Up to 400 Albanians were reported to have stormed aboard a merchant ship in Durres and forced it to set sail for the southern Italian port of Brindisi, which it was approaching under an Italian navy escort.

Unlike rebels who have seized control of the south in an anti-government uprising sparked by anger over the collapse of pyramid savings schemes, looters in the north appeared to be arming themselves for self-protection.
Rebels in the south say Berisha allowed the pyramid schemes to flourish and did not warn people of the risks. They want him to quit before they hand in their weapons.
A new all-party government demanded by the rebels, and approved by Berisha on Wednesday, was sworn in on Thursday.
Tirana residents woke on Thursday to find the military academy and other arms depots in the area had been looted of weapons and other equipment during the night.
Hundreds of civilians, some armed, raided a large Swiss-owned warehouse in a suburb of Tirana and made off with 650 tonnes of flour in trucks, on donkeys and on bicycles.
Outside the capital the situation was equally chaotic as arms depots were raided, and nearly all able-bodied men were carrying weapons of some sort, many firing them into the air.
